triage.name: Amblyopia
triage.reason: Reduced vision in one eye found on pediatric vision screening; diagnosis by acuity and refractive testing.

demographics: Most common cause of reduced vision in children, affecting roughly 1–4% of children
Usually detected at routine vision screening or a well-child visit
Slightly more common in children born prematurely or with low birth weight

risk_factors.text: Anisometropia (unequal refractive error between the eyes)
High refractive error in one or both eyes
Congenital or early cataract or other media opacity
Family history of amblyopia, strabismus, or childhood need for glasses

family_history: Amblyopia in a parent or sibling
Strabismus in a parent or sibling
Childhood glasses use in a parent or sibling

chief_complaints.text: The school nurse said my vision screening was abnormal
I can't see as well out of one eye
I have to sit close to the TV or hold books very near my face

hpi.onset: Gradual and painless, usually from infancy or early childhood; often first noticed at a routine vision screening or well-child visit
hpi.duration: Present for months to years; typically detected between ages 3 and 6
hpi.progression: Stable or slowly worsening until the underlying cause is treated; vision does not improve on its own once the visual system matures
hpi.quality: Blurred or reduced vision in the affected eye; the eye itself looks normal
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; often the child is unaware because the better eye compensates
aggravating: Covering or patching the good eye, which makes the reduced vision obvious
relieving: Using the good eye; nothing relieves the blur in the affected eye

associated_symptoms.text: Squinting or closing one eye to see
Tilting or turning the head to see better
Poor depth perception or trouble with sports and catching a ball
Frequent eye rubbing or eye strain with near work
Falling behind or difficulty seeing the board at school

pertinent_negatives: Headaches that wake the child from sleep or worsen with Valsalva

positives.text: Head tilting or turning to see

negatives: Poor feeding or failure to thrive

atypical.how_it_differs: Cannot report vision problems; presents with a constant eye turn, poor visual tracking, or an abnormal red reflex on newborn or well-baby screening.
missing_classic_features: Squinting or head tilting reported by the child

atypical.how_it_differs: Older children may describe trouble seeing the board or reading, but often the condition is silent and found only on screening because the good eye compensates.
Amblyopia is usually lifelong from childhood; adults may present with longstanding reduced vision in one eye, sometimes unmasked when the good eye develops cataract or other disease.

general.mild: Well-appearing, alert, no distress; plays and interacts normally
general.moderate: Well-appearing; may squint, close one eye, or tilt the head when looking at distant targets
general.severe: Well-appearing but visibly favors one eye; may turn or tilt the head to fixate; no systemic illness
general.critical: Not applicable; amblyopia is not a critical illness

findings.maneuver: Measure visual acuity in each eye separately (age-appropriate chart, or fixation preference in preverbal children) with the other eye occluded
findings.finding: Reduced best-corrected acuity in one eye (or both) compared with the fellow eye

findings.maneuver: Compare acuity between the two eyes with each eye tested alone
findings.finding: Two or more lines of difference between the eyes, or a fixation preference for one eye in a preverbal child

findings.maneuver: Perform the cover-uncover and alternate cover test while the patient fixates on a target
findings.finding: Manifest or latent ocular misalignment (esotropia or exotropia) with refixation movement

findings.maneuver: Perform cycloplegic retinoscopy or autorefraction after cycloplegia
findings.finding: Anisometropia or significant refractive error in the amblyopic eye

findings.maneuver: Check pupillary size, symmetry, and reactivity to light
findings.finding: Equal, round, reactive pupils with no afferent pupillary defect

findings.maneuver: Shine the ophthalmoscope light into each eye and compare the red reflex
findings.finding: Symmetric red reflex with no leukocoria or opacity

findings.maneuver: Inspect the eyelids, conjunctiva, cornea, and lens with a light and ophthalmoscope
findings.finding: Clear cornea and lens, no cataract, ptosis, or media opacity
Normal optic disc, macula, vessels, and peripheral retina

findings.maneuver: Test ductions and versions in all gaze directions
findings.finding: Full, conjugate eye movements without restriction or palsy

findings.maneuver: Confrontation visual fields in each eye
findings.finding: Full visual fields without a defect

findings.maneuver: Perform a brief cranial nerve, motor, sensory, coordination, and gait examination
findings.finding: No focal neurologic deficits, no papilledema, normal gait and coordination

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the head and face
findings.finding: No craniofacial asymmetry, plagiocephaly, or orbital abnormality

imaging.study: MRI brain and orbits with and without IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Atypical features: suspected intracranial or optic pathway lesion, nystagmus, optic atrophy, or neurologic findings

findings.text: Normal brain, optic nerves, chiasm, and orbits
Intracranial mass, hydrocephalus, or optic pathway glioma (alternative diagnosis)

imaging.preferred_when: Urgent evaluation when MRI is unavailable or contraindicated and a structural cause is suspected

initial.test: Visual acuity testing with age-appropriate chart (each eye separately)
initial.why: Detects reduced acuity and interocular difference; the core diagnostic measurement
Identifies strabismus, a common cause of amblyopia
Detects anisometropia and significant refractive error
Screens for media opacity such as cataract or leukocoria
Evaluates optic nerve, macula, and retina for structural causes
Assesses for strabismus and restriction or palsy

confirmatory.test: Cycloplegic refraction with best-corrected visual acuity
confirmatory.why: Confirms amblyopia by showing reduced acuity not fully explained by refractive error alone and identifies treatable refractive causes

supporting.test: MRI brain and orbits with and without IV contrast
supporting.why: Rules out intracranial or optic pathway pathology
supporting.only_if: atypical features such as nystagmus, optic atrophy, neurologic findings, or poor response to treatment

supporting.why: Alternative structural imaging when MRI is unavailable or contraindicated
supporting.only_if: urgent concern for structural lesion and MRI not feasible

not_indicated.test: MRI brain and orbits with and without IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Not routine for typical amblyopia with a clear refractive or strabismic cause
Not routine; radiation exposure without benefit in typical cases

decision_points: Any child with reduced acuity or interocular difference should have cycloplegic refraction before attributing vision loss to amblyopia
Leukocoria, optic atrophy, nystagmus, or neurologic findings warrant urgent imaging and ophthalmology referral
Amblyopia treatment is most effective before age 7–9; early detection and referral are critical

differential.name: Retinoblastoma
differential.why_considered: Reduced vision in one eye in a young child; a white pupil may be mistaken for a lazy eye
differential.trigger: Leukocoria, a white pupillary reflex, or a family history of retinoblastoma

history: White or yellow pupil noticed in photos or by a caregiver
Eye turning in or out that appeared in the first year of life
exam: Possible orbital mass or proptosis in advanced disease
labs: Genetic testing for RB1 mutation when clinical suspicion is high
imaging: Intraocular mass with calcification on ocular ultrasound or MRI of the orbits

differential.name: Congenital cataract
differential.why_considered: Clouding of the lens causes reduced vision and can produce amblyopia if not treated early
differential.trigger: An absent or asymmetric red reflex in a newborn or infant

history: Abnormal red reflex noted on newborn screening
exam: White or dull lens opacity seen through the pupil
Poor visual tracking in an infant
imaging: Lens opacity confirmed on slit-lamp or handheld examination
Ocular ultrasound if the view is obscured

differential.name: Optic nerve glioma
differential.why_considered: A tumor of the optic pathway can cause reduced vision in one eye in a child
differential.trigger: Reduced vision with optic disc pallor, nystagmus, or signs of neurofibromatosis type 1

history: Progressive rather than stable vision loss
Café-au-lait spots or family history of neurofibromatosis type 1
imaging: Enlarged or enhancing optic nerve on MRI of the brain and orbits

differential.name: Strabismus
differential.why_considered: Misaligned eyes are a leading cause of amblyopia and often the reason a child is referred

history: Eye turning in or out noticed by caregivers
exam: Manifest deviation on cover-uncover or alternate cover test
Refixation movement when the fixating eye is covered
Reduced acuity in the deviating eye if amblyopia has developed

differential.name: Anisometropia
differential.why_considered: Unequal refractive error between the eyes is a common cause of amblyopia and can present as reduced vision in one eye

history: No eye turn; vision is reduced in one eye only
Child holds objects close or sits near the television
Family history of childhood glasses use
exam: Reduced acuity in one eye that improves with corrective lenses
Cycloplegic retinoscopy shows a significant difference between eyes

differential.name: Refractive error
differential.why_considered: Nearsightedness, farsightedness, or astigmatism can reduce vision and be mistaken for amblyopia

history: Blurred vision at distance or near

differential.name: Cerebral visual impairment
differential.why_considered: Brain injury from prematurity, hypoxia, or seizures can cause reduced vision that is not explained by eye pathology

exam: Normal ocular structures with reduced vision
Visual inattention or difficulty with crowded scenes
imaging: Periventricular leukomalacia or other brain injury on MRI

severity.mild: Reduced acuity in one eye with a small interocular difference (about 2 lines) and a clear refractive or strabismic cause; responds well to glasses, patching, or atropine
severity.moderate: Marked interocular difference (3 or more lines) or acuity worse than 20/40 in the amblyopic eye; requires several months of occlusion or atropine therapy
severity.severe: Acuity 20/100 or worse in the amblyopic eye, dense deprivation from cataract or media opacity, or amblyopia that persists after initial therapy; may need surgery and prolonged treatment
severity.critical: Not applicable; amblyopia itself is not a life-threatening condition

red_flags.finding: Leukocoria or an absent red reflex
red_flags.meaning: Suggests retinoblastoma, congenital cataract, or another serious intraocular cause; needs urgent ophthalmology evaluation
Suggests optic nerve disease or increased intracranial pressure; requires urgent imaging
Indicates optic nerve or severe retinal dysfunction; not typical of simple amblyopia
Suggests bilateral visual pathway disease or neurologic disorder; needs urgent workup

red_flags.finding: Headaches that wake the child, vomiting, or focal neurologic deficits
red_flags.meaning: Raises concern for an intracranial mass or hydrocephalus; requires urgent imaging

red_flags.finding: Progressive vision loss rather than stable reduced vision
red_flags.meaning: Suggests an active organic cause such as tumor, inflammation, or retinal disease

complications.name: Permanent visual impairment in the amblyopic eye
clues: Poor adherence to patching or atropine

complications.name: Loss of depth perception and stereoacuity
clues: Difficulty with sports or catching a ball

complications.name: Recurrence of amblyopia after treatment
clues: Stopping patching or atropine too early
Return of the interocular acuity difference on follow-up

complications.name: Blindness in the better eye from later injury or disease
clues: Trauma or disease affecting the previously good eye
Sudden loss of vision in the non-amblyopic eye

special_populations.differences: Cannot report vision problems; detected by abnormal red reflex, poor fixation, or a constant eye turn. Treatment must start early because the visual system is still developing.
Most common age group; often found on routine screening. Treatment is most effective before age 7–9, and adherence to patching or atropine is a major determinant of outcome.
Amblyopia is usually lifelong from childhood; adults may present when the good eye develops cataract, macular degeneration, or other disease, unmasking longstanding reduced vision.

key_questions.question: Did the vision screening at school or the well-child visit show a problem in one eye?
key_questions.looking_for: Abnormal screening result or an interocular difference in acuity, the usual way amblyopia is found

key_questions.question: Have you or anyone noticed one eye turning in or out?
key_questions.looking_for: Strabismus, a leading cause of amblyopia

key_questions.question: Does your child squint, close one eye, or tilt or turn the head to see things?
key_questions.looking_for: Compensatory behaviors suggesting reduced vision in one eye

key_questions.question: Does your child hold books very close, sit near the television, or have trouble seeing the board at school?
Has your child ever had a white or cloudy pupil, or an abnormal red reflex noted on a checkup or in a photograph?
key_questions.looking_for: Leukocoria or media opacity suggesting cataract, retinoblastoma, or another serious cause

key_questions.question: Is the vision problem getting worse over time, or has it been stable?
key_questions.looking_for: Progressive loss suggests an active organic cause rather than stable amblyopia

key_questions.question: Any headaches, morning vomiting, or problems with walking, balance, or weakness?
key_questions.looking_for: Signs of raised intracranial pressure or a neurologic lesion

key_questions.question: Was your child born early or with a low birth weight?
key_questions.looking_for: Prematurity or low birth weight, which raise the risk of amblyopia and cerebral visual impairment

key_questions.question: Has your child been diagnosed with any eye condition, or had eye surgery or eye trauma?
key_questions.looking_for: Cataract, ptosis, prior eye surgery, or injury that could cause deprivation amblyopia

key_questions.question: Does anyone in the family have amblyopia, a turned eye, or need for glasses in childhood?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of amblyopia, strabismus, or childhood refractive error

key_questions.question: Does your child take any medications, and are there any medication allergies?
key_questions.looking_for: Medications or allergies that could affect treatment choices such as atropine

key_questions.question: Has your child had any recent fever, illness, or eye redness or discharge?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests infection or another acute cause rather than amblyopia

reasoning_points: Reduced best-corrected visual acuity in one eye, or a two-or-more-line interocular difference, found on screening or examination
A plausible amblyogenic cause: strabismus, anisometropia, high refractive error, or a media opacity such as cataract
The eye appears structurally normal on examination, with a normal red reflex, pupils, and fundus
Vision does not fully correct with refraction alone, distinguishing amblyopia from simple refractive error
No red flags: no leukocoria, afferent pupillary defect, optic disc pallor or swelling, nystagmus, or neurologic findings
The history is gradual and painless, without acute vision loss, eye pain, or systemic illness
Age at presentation is consistent with a developmental visual disorder, typically detected between ages 3 and 6

easy: Preschool child with an abnormal vision screening and a clear interocular acuity difference
Visible eye turn (strabismus) with reduced acuity in the deviating eye
Normal eye examination otherwise, with a normal red reflex and fundus
Improves with glasses and patching or atropine
medium: No visible eye turn; reduced acuity found only on careful separate-eye testing
Anisometropia detected on cycloplegic refraction as the underlying cause
Child who does not complain because the good eye compensates
Older child with trouble seeing the board mistaken for simple nearsightedness
hard: Preverbal infant with poor fixation or a constant eye turn and no reported symptoms
Bilateral amblyopia from high refractive error in both eyes
Deprivation amblyopia from a subtle cataract or ptosis with a mildly abnormal red reflex
Reduced vision with optic disc pallor or nystagmus suggesting an alternative diagnosis such as optic pathway glioma or cerebral visual impairment
Amblyopia unmasked in an adult when the good eye develops cataract or other disease
